pool.note: Tie prose; {A}/{B} are the tie parties (guaranteed, not atoms); the parties' categories (economy/criminal/military/religious/magic/government) are the archetype's tie rule, so a line about {B}'s operation, {A}'s pulpit/altar/congregation or {B}'s company presumes the party's role, not a record atom. keyDeclares from priorityHelpers.js stress flags: econ_crim_* only under merchantCriminalBlur (hasMerchantGuild && hasCriminalInst); rel_mil_crusader only under crusaderSynthesis (hasGarrison && hasChurch; hasChurch also matches monastery/priest, so temple is NOT key-guaranteed and the 'shrine' lines declare it); rel_crim_fraud under religiousFraud (hasChurch && hasCriminalInst); mag_crim_market under arcaneBlackMarket (hasMagicInst, which includes alchemist, && hasCriminalInst). mil_crim_corruption is reachable without stateCrime, so garrison is not key-guaranteed there. FORCE WORDS substituted per place by forceWordsOf (rendered as default garrison words, treated as substituted, not atoms): mil_crim_corruption.tension#7, econ_mil_contract.desc#5, rel_mil_crusader.desc#1/#3/#4, tension#3/#6, gov_mil_friction.desc#3, tension#3/#7. LITERAL force words that are NOT substituted and are declared: 'The watch reports' (mil_crim_corruption.desc#5), 'under the watch's command' (econ_mil_contract.tension#6), 'the watch ... the barracks' (gov_mil_friction.desc#5). 'ruler: council' is used for lines presuming a governing council exists here (before the council, council session/bloc/committee, a councillor's son, {A}'s council); a presence atom 'council' would be more exact (a council may sit under another ruler kind) -- reported. INEXPRESSIBLE (colour:false, empty arrays): customs house/customs officer (econ_crim_blur.desc#3, tension#4); magistrate/court/a case judged (econ_crim_exploitation.tension#6, mil_crim_suppression.tension#3, bitter_history.desc#3, tension#3, rel_mil_crusader.tension#6 church trial/court-martial); 'the capital' = an overlord realm (gov_mil_friction.tension#2, #5); an expected riot, unrest-like but not a crisis kind (gov_mil_friction.tension#6); a hired mercenary company (econ_mil_contract.desc#0 and the archetype generally: no mercenary atom). Season presumptions (no atom): 'two winters' (mil_crim_suppression.desc#7), midsummer (gov_econ_dependence.tension#1, peer_rivalry.tension#4), winter grain stores (gov_econ_dependence.tension#7). LABELS 'Mentor and Successor', 'Professional Rivalry', 'Jurisdictional Tension' presume a relation between the two parties (shared trade/office; two offices, civil vs military) -- handled by a tie rule, not a record atom.

rows.text: Commercial Complicity
{A} and {B} maintain a relationship that exists in legal grey territory. {A} provides legitimate cover, {B} ensures market access that official channels wouldn't permit.
The books of {A} are clean because {B} keeps certain entries off them; the arrangement benefits both parties and would survive scrutiny by neither.
What {A} sells is respectability, and {B} is a steady customer. Goods move through channels no inspector has thought to draw on a map.
{A} signs the import papers and {B} decides what is actually in the crates. The warehouse keeps two inventories, and only one is shown to the customs house.
{B}'s money buys {A}'s stock at full price and sells it back through stalls that pay no market dues. Both of them call it a partnership.
{A}'s shop front is real, the trade is real, and a third of the coin that passes through it belongs to {B}.
{A} vouches for {B}'s people at the guild hall. In return, {B}'s people keep {A}'s carts moving on roads where other carts are stopped.
{A} holds the licence, {B} supplies the goods, and the profit is split in a back room on the first of every month.
If either is investigated, the other is implicated. Both know this. Neither mentions it.
A clerk has begun cross-referencing the ledgers. Neither party has decided what to do about it.
One profitable season more, {A} keeps saying. The seasons keep being profitable.
{B} wants to move a larger cargo through {A}'s warehouse next month. {A} has not agreed and has not refused.
A customs officer has asked {A} for the names of every supplier. {B}'s name is missing from the list, and the officer has noticed the gap.
{A} has started paying off the guild debts that tied the two of them together. {B} reads it as a plan to leave.
{B} has been seen at {A}'s counting-house in daylight. That was never part of the arrangement.
{A}'s eldest has found the second ledger and asked what {B}'s initials mean.
Protection Arrangement
{B}'s operation charges {A} a "security fee" that is, in practice, a protection racket. {A} pays without complaint because the alternative is worse.
Every month {A} pays {B} for protection against dangers that would, on inspection, trace back to {B}. Both sides account for it as a cost of doing business.
The "security fee" {B} collects from {A} buys exactly one thing: the absence of {B}. It is paid punctually.
{A} pays {B} a tenth of every sale. The one season {A} paid late, a storehouse burned.
{B}'s collectors visit {A} on the same day each month and leave with a sealed purse. Nobody in the street watches them go.
{A} owes {B} for protection that was never asked for and cannot be cancelled. The debt is renewed in person, at the door.
{B} sets the fee, {A} pays it, and the price goes on every customer's bill without a line of its own.
{A}'s premises are the only ones on the row that have never been robbed. {B} reminds {A} of this when the fee is due.
{A} is quietly documenting every payment. Someone is being prepared for a fall.
The fee went up this quarter without explanation. {A}'s patience is a finite ledger.
A rival crew has offered {A} a better rate. Accepting would be a declaration of war on {B}.
{A} has hired two guards of their own. {B} has asked, politely, what they are for.
{B} wants a cut of {A}'s new venture before it opens. The fee was never meant to grow with the business.
{A} missed this month's payment by three days. {B} has not sent anyone yet, and that is worse.
{A} has written to the magistrate about {B}'s collectors. The letter sits unsent in {A}'s desk.
{B}'s collector was found drunk with {A}'s purse still sealed. Someone will have to explain the delay to {B}.
Corrupt Arrangement
{A} receives regular payments from {B}'s organization in exchange for patrol schedules and advance notice of raids. Both maintain professional courtesy in public.
{B}'s operation runs on a schedule {A} provides: patrols that turn a street early, raids announced a day in advance. In public the two exchange formal nods.
{A}'s clearance record looks respectable because {B} decides which crimes get cleared. The price of the arrangement is itemised and paid on time.
{A} takes {B}'s silver every quarter day and keeps certain doors unwatched in return. Each treats the other as a reliable colleague.
{B}'s people are never searched on {A}'s watch. The arrangement is three years old and has never been put in writing.
{A} warns {B} before every raid and arrests the competitors {B} names. The watch reports show a fine record of arrests.
When {B}'s crew needs a prisoner released, {A} signs the order. When {A} needs an arrest, {B} supplies the culprit.
{A} commands the patrols and {B} pays for their routes. The streets {B} uses are the quietest in the settlement.
A new superior has started asking uncomfortable questions about clearance rates. One of them will have to act before the other does.
An honest sergeant has been transferred into {A}'s command. Both parties consider this a problem.
The payments have started arriving late. In this trade, late is a message.
{A} was promoted last month, and {B} expects the price of silence to stay the same. {A} does not.
One of {B}'s runners was arrested by a patrol {A} did not assign. The runner knows both their names.
{B} has asked {A} to lose a piece of evidence that three other officers have already seen.
{A}'s quarter-day payment from {B} arrived with a name attached: someone {B} wants arrested.
An auditor from the garrison is counting {A}'s arrest records against the coin in {A}'s house. {B} is watching the count.
Active Suppression
{A} has made dismantling {B}'s operation a personal priority. The feeling is mutual.
{A} keeps a file on {B}'s operation that grows by the week; {B} keeps one on {A} that is already complete.
The war between {A} and {B} is fought in raids, informants, and paperwork. Neither side counts it as winnable; neither will stop.
{A} has closed three of {B}'s houses this year. {B} has opened four.
{A} wants {B} in a cell and has said so before the council. {B} has answered by paying two of {A}'s informants.
{B}'s people know {A}'s patrol routes by heart, and {A}'s people know which taverns {B} uses. Neither side has made the arrest that counts.
{A} and {B} are open enemies. Every raid {A} orders costs {B} money, and every month {B} survives costs {A} standing.
{A} hunts {B}'s operation street by street, and {B} moves it one street ahead. The chase has lasted two winters.
{B} has leverage on someone close to {A}. It hasn't been used yet.
{A} is one warrant away from a raid that would end it. The warrant keeps not being signed.
Someone in {A}'s command reports to {B}. The file says so; it does not say who.
{A} has a witness willing to name {B} before a magistrate. {B} knows where the witness lives.
{B} has offered {A} a truce and a purse. {A} has not answered, which {B} counts as progress.
{A}'s best informant inside {B}'s crew has stopped reporting. Nobody has seen the informant for nine days.
{B} has hired an advocate to sue {A} over the last raid. The case comes before the council this season.
{A} has been ordered to stand down against {B} by someone above {A}. The order did not say why.
Security Contract
{B}'s company is retained by {A}'s interests on an exclusive basis. The arrangement works well enough that official channels have stopped asking questions.
{A} pays {B}'s company well and exclusively, and in return certain cargoes move unescorted and uninspected. The arrangement predates every official who might question it.
The contract between {A} and {B} is renewed annually with a handshake; what it actually covers has never been written down anywhere.
{B}'s company guards {A}'s warehouses and wagons for a fixed fee each season. {A} pays on time and asks for nothing in writing.
{A} is {B}'s largest client and {B} is {A}'s only protection. Each would be badly hurt by losing the other.
{B}'s soldiers wear {A}'s colours on the road and take {A}'s orders without question. No magistrate has a say over them.
{A} hired {B}'s company after the last caravan was lost. No caravan has been lost since, and {B}'s fee has doubled.
{B} answers to {A}'s purse before any other authority. Everyone in the settlement knows which way {B}'s company would march.
The contract is up for renewal. {B} has been approached by a competitor. {A} doesn't know yet.
{B}'s men have started asking what exactly they are guarding. {A} prefers them incurious.
The last shipment was short, and each side privately blames the other. The next one will settle the question.
{A} has cut {B}'s fee by a fifth. {B}'s company still guards the wagons, but more slowly.
{B}'s company has taken on a second client, and {A} has learned the client's name.
A guard from {B}'s company was killed protecting {A}'s cargo. {B} wants compensation the contract does not mention.
The council wants {B}'s company under the watch's command. {A} loses the contract's whole value if it agrees.
{A} has asked {B} to escort a cargo with no manifest. {B} has named a price.
Sacred Commission
{A} and {B} operate as a unified authority: temporal and spiritual power reinforcing each other. Dissent against one is dissent against both.
Between {A}'s pulpit and {B}'s garrison, the settlement is governed twice over; the sermons and the patrol routes have a way of agreeing.
{A} blesses what {B} enforces, and {B} enforces what {A} blesses. Where one authority ends and the other begins is a question neither permits.
{A} preaches the cause and {B} raises the men. The shrine's coffers pay for the garrison's swords.
{B}'s soldiers take their oaths before {A}'s altar. To {A}'s faithful, {B}'s orders carry the weight of scripture.
{A} names the settlement's enemies from the pulpit, and {B} rides against them within the week.
{A} and {B} hold the settlement between faith and force. The two of them meet after every service to agree the week's orders.
{B} carries {A}'s banner on every patrol. Crossing {B} is treated as heresy, and heresy is punished by {B}.
They disagree on a fundamental question of method that neither will put into writing.
A penitent has brought a case that pits doctrine against order. It has not been resolved. It will not stay private.
The crowd that obeys them both has begun to notice it is one crowd. So has {B}.
{A} has declared a holy day on which no soldier may bear arms. {B} has a patrol scheduled for it.
{B}'s men have started praying at a different shrine. {A} counts the empty places at every service.
{A} wants an armed march against a rival sect. {B} has counted the cost in men and wants to wait a year.
A soldier under {B} stands accused of sacrilege. {A} demands a church trial; {B} wants a court-martial.
{B} has started giving orders in the name of the faith without consulting {A}.
Institutional Cover
{A}'s religious position provides {B}'s operation with legitimacy, meeting spaces, and an excuse for financial flows that would otherwise attract scrutiny.
{B}'s money passes through {A}'s offertory and comes out consecrated; the meeting rooms are sanctified, the accounts are not examined.
{A} provides the sanctity, {B} provides the income, and the congregation provides the cover (unknowingly), which is what makes it work.
{B}'s crew meets in the crypt beneath {A}'s shrine after evening prayers. {A} keeps the only key.
{A} records {B}'s payments as gifts from a pious donor. The donor has never attended a service.
{B} funds {A}'s alms, and {A} vouches for {B}'s good character to anyone who asks. Both are paid in the same coin.
{A}'s charity runs the soup kitchen, and {B}'s couriers collect their parcels from the kitchen's back door.
{A} hears {B}'s confession each week and keeps {B}'s accounts each month. Neither duty is written down.
{A} has a genuine crisis of conscience that {B} is not prepared to accommodate.
A visiting cleric has asked to audit the shrine's books. {B} has offered to handle it.
{A} has started keeping a second set of records. Confession, of a kind.
A member of {A}'s congregation saw {B}'s men carrying crates out of the shrine at night, and has asked {A} about it twice.
{B} wants to store weapons beneath {A}'s altar. {A} has refused once and been asked again.
{A}'s superior is coming to inspect the shrine's accounts. {B}'s gifts make up half the income.
{A} preached a sermon on theft last week. {B} took it personally.
{B} has asked {A} to marry two of the crew under false names. {A} has not set a date.
Arcane Supplier
{A} provides {B}'s network with components, identification services, and the occasional forged document that only a skilled practitioner could produce.
When {B}'s network needs a seal copied, a face forgotten, or a document aged thirty years, the work arrives through {A} and is never signed.
{A} takes commissions from {B} that no guild register records: small workings, expertly done, each one deniable and none of them innocent.
{A} brews what {B} sells: sleeping draughts, truth-tinctures, and inks that vanish after a day.
{B} brings {A} the jobs and the payment, and {A} asks no questions about who the work is for.
{A}'s workshop has a back door, and {B}'s couriers are the only ones who use it.
{A} supplies {B}'s network with wards against detection. Each ward is sold at triple the guild price.
{B} pays {A} a retainer to be ready at any hour. Twice this year, {A} has been called out before dawn.
The last commission left traces that a determined investigator might find. {A} is reconsidering the relationship.
{B} has begun asking for workings of a different order: the kind with witnesses. {A} has not yet said no.
Another practitioner has noticed {A}'s signature in the residue. Professional courtesy has limits.
{A}'s apprentice has started asking where the night commissions go. {B} has noticed the apprentice.
{B} owes {A} for three months of work and has offered information instead of coin.
A ward {A} made for {B} failed during a robbery. {B} blames the ward; {A} blames the thief.
The guild has summoned {A} to explain a shortfall in licensed components. {B}'s orders account for the missing stock.
{A} has been offered a guild post that requires a clean record. {B} has a list of everything {A} has made.
Financial Dependence
The settlement's civic functions run on credit extended by {B}. {A} cannot take any action that seriously threatens {B}'s interests, and {B} does not let this be forgotten.
{B} holds the settlement's debts and therefore, in every way that matters, its agenda; {A} governs within the margin {B} allows.
Every civic project {A} announces has first been costed, quietly, in {B}'s counting-room. The public believes the order is the other way around.
{A}'s treasury borrowed from {B} to cover a bad harvest and has borrowed every year since. The interest is paid before the wages.
{B} holds the settlement's tax rolls as security for its loans. {A} cannot raise a levy without {B}'s clerks counting it first.
{A} owes {B} more than the settlement collects in two years of taxes. {B} is paid first, every quarter.
{B} lends and {A} spends. The council's decisions are made in {A}'s chamber and approved in {B}'s counting-house.
{A} governs on {B}'s credit. Every loan renewed adds one more condition to the next.
{A} has identified an alternative creditor. {B} has heard the same rumour.
The interest falls due at midsummer and the treasury will not cover it. {B} has already drafted the terms of the extension.
A faction on the council wants the debt repudiated outright. {A} has stopped disagreeing in public.
{B} has asked for a seat on the council as a condition of the next loan. {A} has three weeks to answer.
{A} has proposed a new tax to clear the debt. {B}'s friends on the council will vote against it.
{B} is calling in a third of the debt at once. {A} has until the next quarter day to find it.
{A} has started borrowing small sums from {B}'s rivals. {B}'s clerks have seen the receipts.
{B} has refused credit for the winter grain stores. {A} must choose between the creditor and the granary.
Jurisdictional Tension
{A} and {B} disagree fundamentally about where civil authority ends and military authority begins. The argument has been running for years and occasionally generates paperwork.
{A} issues orders {B} regards as suggestions, and {B} takes actions {A} regards as insubordination; the settlement runs in the gap between.
The line between {A}'s authority and {B}'s has been redrawn four times and honoured never. Each keeps the map that favours them.
{A} controls the garrison's pay and {B} controls its swords. Each uses their half to bargain for the other's.
{B} reports to {A} on paper and to no one in practice. {A} has three letters of complaint unanswered.
{A} wants the watch under civil command; {B} wants the council out of the barracks. They meet monthly and settle nothing.
{A} sets the curfew and {B} decides whether to enforce it. The two have not agreed on a curfew in a year.
{B} answers {A}'s summons late and leaves early. {A} now issues them in writing so the delays are on record.
An incident is coming that will force the issue. Both are positioning for it.
A prisoner is currently held by both jurisdictions at once. Neither will release the paperwork first.
{B} has begun drilling in the square without asking. {A} has begun writing letters to the capital.
{A} has cut the garrison's pay to fund the market repairs. {B} has told the soldiers who signed the order.
{B} arrested a councillor's son without {A}'s warrant. {A} has demanded his release by tomorrow.
{A} has asked the capital to replace {B}. {B} has asked the capital to dissolve {A}'s council.
A riot is expected on the next market day, and {A} and {B} have issued opposite orders for it.
{B} has begun collecting a road toll for the garrison. {A} calls it theft from the treasury.
Professional Rivalry
{A} and {B} compete for the same resource, position, or reputation. The competition is vigorous but bounded. Neither has crossed the line into genuine enmity. Yet.
{A} and {B} want the same thing and cannot both have it. The contest is conducted with scrupulous courtesy and total commitment.
Every advance {A} makes is answered by {B} within the season; the rivalry has become its own institution, with rules neither wrote and both obey.
{A} and {B} bid for the same contracts and sit at the same tables. Each counts the other's wins more carefully than their own.
{A} and {B} trained together and have competed ever since. The settlement keeps score, and so do they.
{A} wants {B}'s position, and {B} wants {A}'s reputation. They are civil in public and unforgiving in private.
Every client {A} wins is one {B} lost, and the reverse. The two keep a polite distance and an exact tally.
{A} and {B} are rivals for the same patron's favour. Each has spent the year trying to be first through the patron's door.
A decision coming in the next season will advantage one significantly. The other knows this.
A mutual patron has let it be known there is room for only one of them at the next table.
One of them has recently broken an unwritten rule of the contest. The other is deciding what that permits.
{A} has hired away {B}'s best assistant. {B} has said nothing about it, to anyone.
A post opens at midsummer, and only {A} or {B} can fill it.
{B} has been telling clients that {A}'s work is slipping. Two of the clients have repeated it to {A}.
{A} and {B} will both present proposals at the next council session. Only one will be accepted.
{A} lost the last contract to {B} by a single vote, and has learned who cast it.
Mentor and Successor
{A} shaped {B}'s career in ways that {B} has not fully acknowledged. The debt is real; the gratitude is complicated.
{B} stands where {A} put them, by a ladder {A} built and {B} has since pulled up. Both remember it differently.
What {B} knows, {A} taught (including, inconveniently, how to outmanoeuvre a teacher).
{A} took {B} in as an apprentice and taught them the trade, the clients, and the names worth knowing.
{B} learned the work at {A}'s side for seven years. Half of {B}'s clients first came through {A}'s door.
{A} vouched for {B} when nobody else would. {B}'s first post came from that word.
{B} still uses {A}'s methods and {A}'s ledger format. Everyone who sees {B}'s work recognises the teacher.
{A} named {B} as successor in front of witnesses. The formal handover has not happened.
{B} now operates in ways {A} would not approve of. Neither discusses the divergence directly.
{A} has one favour left to call in, and is saving it. {B} knows, and is watching for it.
A third party has asked {A}, quietly, whether {B} can be trusted. The answer took too long.
{B} has taken on a client {A} turned away on principle.
{A} has taken a new apprentice, and {B} has heard the apprentice is being taught things {B} never was.
{B} corrected {A} in public last month, and was right.
{A} has asked {B} for a loan. It is the first time a debt between teacher and student has run that way.
{B} has begun teaching {A}'s methods as {B}'s own.
Mutual Leverage
{A} and {B} each hold information or resources the other needs. They cooperate efficiently and neither trusts the other at all.
What {A} knows would ruin {B}; what {B} holds would finish {A}. On this foundation they have built an excellent working relationship.
{A} and {B} deal with each other like men carrying lit lanterns in a powder store, carefully, and with great mutual politeness.
{A} and {B} trade favours on a strict count. Neither has ever been more than one favour ahead.
{A} controls a vote {B} needs, and {B} controls a supply {A} needs. Their meetings are short and their bargains hold.
{A} and {B} each have something to trade and nothing to give away. They meet in private, bargain hard, and keep every bargain.
{B} needs {A}'s seal on certain papers; {A} needs {B}'s silence about certain others. Neither has asked for more than the other could pay.
{A} and {B} sit on opposite sides of most questions and vote together on the few that touch their shared interests.
The balance of leverage has recently shifted. One party has noticed; the other hasn't yet.
A document each believed only they possessed has surfaced in a third set of hands.
{B} has recently secured something that makes {A}'s hold obsolete. The politeness continues, for now.
{A} has asked {B} for a second favour before repaying the first.
{B} has found a new source for what {A} supplies. {A} has not been told.
The vote {B} needs from {A} comes up next week, and {A} has named a new price.
{A}'s secret is about to come out by other means. Once it does, {B} holds nothing over {A}.
{B} has written down what {A} owes and left a copy with a notary.
Pragmatic Alliance
{A} and {B} work together because the alternative (working against each other) is worse for both. The alliance holds as long as the calculation holds.
{A} and {B} are allies by arithmetic: each has counted the cost of the other as an enemy and found it too high. The friendship is warm, public, and entirely conditional.
The alliance between {A} and {B} was born of a shared threat and has outlived it; both are quietly recalculating what it is now for.
{A} and {B} share a council bloc and a list of enemies. They do not share their plans.
{A} and {B} back each other in public and check each other's work in private.
{A} brings the votes and {B} brings the money. The alliance is three years old and has won every vote it needed.
{A} and {B} signed a pact after their last quarrel cost them both. They keep to its terms exactly.
{A} and {B} are allies with separate interests. They meet to coordinate and leave by different doors.
A third party is actively working to change that calculation.
The threat that made the alliance necessary is gone. Neither has said so aloud.
{A} has taken a precaution against {B} that {B} was not meant to discover. {B} has discovered it.
{B} has been dining with {A}'s rivals. {A} heard about it from a servant.
{A} wants to bring a third member into the alliance. {B} thinks the newcomer would take {B}'s place.
{B} voted against {A} on a small matter last week. {A} is waiting to see whether it was small.
{A} and {B} both want the same office, and the alliance cannot survive one of them winning it.
{B} has asked {A} to back a candidate {A} distrusts. Refusing would cost the alliance its majority.
Genuine Respect
{A} and {B} have earned each other's regard through demonstrated competence. They don't agree on everything but they trust each other's judgment within their respective domains.
{A} and {B} disagree often and trust completely. Each has watched the other be right at cost, and neither forgets it.
There is no arrangement between {A} and {B}, only a long record of kept words; in this settlement that makes them remarkable.
{A} sends difficult cases to {B}, and {B} sends them back solved. Neither has ever charged the other a fee.
{A} and {B} have stood on opposite sides of three disputes and praised each other after every one.
{B} once told the council that {A} was right and {B} was wrong. {A} has not forgotten it.
{A} and {B} consult each other before any decision that matters. The advice is honest and is always taken seriously.
{A} trusts {B}'s word over any written contract. {B} has never given a reason to regret it.
They are about to be on opposite sides of a significant decision.
One of them is being pressured to act against the other, and has not yet mentioned it.
The respect is real and the interests are diverging. Both can read a map.
{A} has learned something about {B}'s family that {B} does not know.
{B} has been offered {A}'s post by people who want {A} gone.
{A} has made a mistake that {B} is bound to report. {B} has not reported it.
The council has asked {A} and {B} to audit each other's accounts. Both agreed, and neither is comfortable.
{B} has publicly backed a plan that {A} thinks will fail. {A} has said so once, in private.
Outstanding Debt
{A} owes {B} something significant: a favour, a secret kept, a crisis managed. The debt has never been formally acknowledged. It doesn't need to be.
Years ago {B} did for {A} the kind of favour that cannot be repaid, only serviced. {A} has been servicing it ever since.
Between {A} and {B} stands an old kindness with the structure of a mortgage. Neither names it; both know the balance to the penny.
{B} paid {A}'s bail eleven years ago and has never mentioned it. {A} mentions it to no one.
{A} owes {B} a large sum in coin, borrowed in a bad year and repaid in small amounts ever since.
{B} kept {A}'s name out of a scandal that ruined two others. {A} has voted with {B} ever since.
{B} nursed {A} through a winter fever when no one else would come. {A} still owes the debt and still knows it.
{A} borrowed {B}'s good name to win a post. {B} has never asked for it back.
{B} is about to call it in.
